_link.title: I can identify the four possible outcomes of a particle collision

toLevel2.stem: How many possible outcomes are there for a particle collision?
distractors: Two
Three
Six

toLevel2.stem: Which combination of factors leads to a successful reaction?
distractors: Incorrect orientation and sufficient energy
Correct orientation and insufficient energy
Incorrect orientation and insufficient energy

toLevel2.stem: How many of the four possible collision outcomes result in a reaction?
distractors: Two
Three
All four

toLevel2.stem: What happens when particles collide with sufficient energy but incorrect orientation?
distractors: A reaction always occurs
A different product is formed
The particles gain more energy

toLevel2.stem: What happens when particles collide with correct orientation but insufficient energy?
distractors: A reaction always occurs
A slower reaction occurs
A partial reaction occurs

toLevel2.stem: Only one of the four possible collision outcomes results in a successful reaction.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A collision with sufficient energy will always result in a reaction regardless of orientation.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: The four outcomes combine two factors: {{blank:1}} (correct or incorrect) and {{blank:2}} (sufficient or insufficient).
distractors: temperature

toLevel2.stem: A successful collision requires both correct {{blank:1}} and sufficient {{blank:2}} — if either is missing, no reaction occurs.

distractors: two

toLevel3.stem: Why do most collisions in a concentrated mixture not result in a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: Three out of four collision outcomes fail due to wrong orientation, insufficient energy, or both
distractors: Concentrated mixtures have particles that cannot collide with each other
All collisions succeed but the products immediately break apart
Concentrated mixtures always have activation energies of zero

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important to understand that only one of four outcomes leads to a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: It explains why reaction rates can be low even when particles collide frequently
distractors: It proves that most reactions cannot occur under any conditions
It shows that collision theory only applies to reactions with four steps
It demonstrates that energy is the only factor affecting reaction rate

toLevel3.stem: Two gas particles with high kinetic energy collide but one approaches from the wrong angle. What is the outcome?
toLevel3.answer: No reaction — despite sufficient energy, incorrect orientation prevents product formation
distractors: A reaction occurs because high kinetic energy overrides orientation
A different product is formed due to the unusual collision angle
The particles fuse together permanently due to the high energy

toLevel3.stem: How do the four collision outcomes relate to the three conditions of collision theory?
toLevel3.answer: The outcomes are the possible combinations of meeting or not meeting the energy and orientation conditions
distractors: The four outcomes are unrelated to the three conditions of collision theory
Each outcome corresponds to one of three conditions plus a bonus condition
The four outcomes replace the three conditions in advanced collision theory

toLevel3.stem: If increasing temperature increases the proportion of particles with sufficient energy, which collision outcomes become more likely?
toLevel3.answer: Outcomes involving sufficient energy become more likely, increasing the chance of a successful reaction
distractors: All four outcomes become equally likely at higher temperatures
Only the outcome with insufficient energy and correct orientation increases
Temperature has no effect on any of the four collision outcomes

toLevel3.stem: Why is the combination of correct orientation AND sufficient energy relatively rare?
toLevel3.answer: Both conditions must be met simultaneously, and each has its own probability of occurring
distractors: Correct orientation and sufficient energy never occur at the same time
Only one particle needs correct orientation, not both particles
Sufficient energy automatically guarantees correct orientation

toLevel3.stem: The four collision outcomes help explain why reaction rates are often low even when collision frequency is high.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Most collisions fail because particles lack correct {{blank:1}}, sufficient {{blank:2}}, or both.
distractors: mass
speed
temperature
pressure

toLevel3.stem: The successful outcome is rare because both conditions must be met {{blank:1}}, and each condition has its own {{blank:2}} of occurring.
distractors: separately
certainty
sequentially
requirement

toLevel3.stem: Increasing temperature makes outcomes involving {{blank:1}} energy more likely, which increases the overall chance of a {{blank:2}} collision.
distractors: insufficient
failed
excess
frequent

toLevel4.stem: A student observes that only 1 in 500 collisions between two gas molecules results in a reaction. Using the four outcomes framework, what can be concluded?
toLevel4.answer: The vast majority of collisions lack correct orientation, sufficient energy, or both
distractors: The gas molecules are too large to collide with each other at all
The activation energy must be zero for this reaction to occur
All 500 collisions have sufficient energy but all lack correct orientation

toLevel4.stem: A student creates a table showing the four outcomes. They list 'correct orientation + insufficient energy = reaction.' What error have they made?
toLevel4.answer: Correct orientation with insufficient energy does NOT produce a reaction — both conditions must be met
distractors: The table is correct — correct orientation always guarantees a reaction
The error is that insufficient energy should be labelled sufficient energy
The error is that correct orientation should be labelled incorrect orientation

toLevel4.stem: In a simulation, a student models 1000 collisions. They find 200 have correct orientation but only 100 have sufficient energy. If orientation and energy are independent, approximately how many successful collisions should occur?
toLevel4.answer: Approximately 20 — 20% have correct orientation × 10% have sufficient energy = 2%
distractors: Approximately 300 — the sum of 200 and 100
Approximately 100 — the smaller of the two numbers
Approximately 200 — the larger of the two numbers

toLevel4.stem: A student increases the temperature of a reaction. Which of the four collision outcomes is most directly affected?
toLevel4.answer: Outcomes involving insufficient energy decrease because more particles now exceed Ea
distractors: Outcomes involving incorrect orientation decrease because heat aligns particles
All four outcomes change equally with any temperature increase
No outcomes are affected because the four possibilities are fixed

toLevel4.stem: A student adds a catalyst to a reaction. How does this change the distribution of collision outcomes?
toLevel4.answer: More collisions now have sufficient energy because Ea is lowered, increasing successful outcomes
distractors: More collisions now have correct orientation because the catalyst aligns particles
The catalyst eliminates all unsuccessful outcomes making every collision successful
The catalyst has no effect on any of the four collision outcomes

toLevel4.stem: A reaction has a very low activation energy but a very strict orientation requirement. What would be the dominant reason for unsuccessful collisions?
toLevel4.answer: Incorrect orientation would be the main reason most collisions fail
distractors: Insufficient energy would be the main reason most collisions fail
Both factors would contribute equally to unsuccessful collisions
All collisions would be successful because the Ea is low

toLevel4.stem: A student classifies a collision as 'incorrect orientation, sufficient energy.' What would they observe at the molecular level?
toLevel4.answer: The particles bounce apart despite having enough energy — the geometry was wrong
distractors: The particles react to form products because they have enough energy
The particles stick together permanently without forming products
The particles slow down and lose all their kinetic energy

toLevel4.stem: Adding a catalyst shifts the distribution of outcomes by making more collisions have {{blank:1}} energy, because Ea is {{blank:2}}.
distractors: insufficient
raised
excess
eliminated

toLevel4.stem: If 20% of collisions have correct orientation and 10% have sufficient energy, approximately {{blank:1}}% of collisions will be {{blank:2}}.
distractors: energetic
oriented

toLevel4.stem: For a reaction with low Ea but strict orientation requirements, the dominant reason for failure is {{blank:1}} orientation, not insufficient {{blank:2}}.
distractors: correct
mass
perfect

toLevel5.stem: Increasing temperature shifts more collisions from 'insufficient energy' to 'sufficient energy' outcomes. However, it does not change orientation probabilities. Analyze why temperature still causes a significant rate increase.
toLevel5.answer: Even without changing orientation, converting more collisions to the 'sufficient energy' category increases the fraction that meets both criteria
distractors: Temperature changes orientation as well, but this effect is too small to measure
Temperature eliminates the orientation requirement entirely at high enough values
Temperature only increases rate by increasing collision frequency, not by changing outcomes

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'Since three out of four outcomes fail, no more than 25% of collisions can ever succeed.' Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — the proportion of successful collisions depends on the actual probabilities of correct orientation and sufficient energy, which vary
distractors: Correct — exactly 25% of all collisions must always be successful
Incorrect — all four outcomes are always equally likely at 25% each
Correct — the maximum success rate is fixed at one-quarter regardless of conditions

toLevel5.stem: For a given reaction, the probability of correct orientation is 5% and the probability of sufficient energy is 1%. Approximately what fraction of collisions result in a reaction?
toLevel5.answer: Approximately 0.05%, since both probabilities multiply together
distractors: Approximately 6%, since both probabilities add together
Approximately 5%, since only orientation matters
Approximately 1%, since only energy matters

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'A catalyst improves orientation, which is why it increases the proportion of successful collisions.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — a catalyst lowers Ea, increasing the proportion with sufficient energy, not improving orientation
distractors: Correct — catalysts work primarily by improving particle alignment
Correct — catalysts rotate particles into the correct orientation
Incorrect — catalysts eliminate all four outcomes and create a new mechanism

toLevel5.stem: Compare a reaction with strict orientation requirements and high Ea to one with flexible orientation and low Ea. Which would have a higher proportion of successful collisions at the same temperature?
toLevel5.answer: The reaction with flexible orientation and low Ea — both factors favour more successful collisions
distractors: The reaction with strict orientation and high Ea — higher energy means more success
Both reactions would have the same proportion of successful collisions
The reaction with strict orientation — it filters out weak collisions

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Since we cannot control orientation, it is a useless concept in chemistry.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — understanding orientation helps explain observed rates and why certain reactions are slow despite low Ea
distractors: Correct — orientation has no practical application in chemistry at all
Correct — only energy matters for reaction rate and orientation is irrelevant
Incorrect — we can control orientation by changing the temperature

toLevel5.stem: In a reaction where the orientation requirement is very flexible (many orientations work), which factor predominantly limits the rate?
toLevel5.answer: The proportion of particles with sufficient energy to exceed Ea
distractors: The orientation requirement, even though it is flexible
The total number of particles in the system
The system being open or closed

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that for a reaction where 50% of orientations are correct and 50% of particles exceed Ea, the success rate would be 100%. Is this correct?
toLevel5.answer: No — the probabilities multiply, giving 25% success rate, not add to give 100%
distractors: Yes — both conditions are met half the time so together they are met every time
No — the success rate would be 0% because neither condition is met fully
Yes — probabilities always add when both conditions are independent

Understanding the four outcomes explains why even {{blank:1}} mixtures can have low reaction rates — most collisions fail due to wrong orientation, insufficient energy, or {{blank:2}}.
